name: Social media dysmorphia (filter dysmorphia / Snapchat dysmorphia)
lead: Social media dysmorphia, also called Snapchat dysmorphia, filter dysmorphia or selfie dysmorphia, is an informal term for the phenomenon of people seeking cosmetic procedures to resemble their filtered or edited selfies, or feeling distress at the gap between their real appearance and edited images of themselves.[1] For anyone working on their looks, the idea matters because it describes how filters shift the reference point: smoother skin, narrower noses and larger eyes become the benchmark, and clinicians say this affects which treatments people request and what they expect from them.[1][2]

It is not a formal diagnosis. Clinicians discuss it in relation to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), an obsessive preoccupation with perceived flaws in appearance. Wikipedia reports that BDD is found in about 24% of patients seeking plastic surgery in one meta-analysis, and that a 2019 systematic review linked appearance-focused social media use to greater body image dissatisfaction.[1][3]

The term was coined by British cosmetic surgeon Tijion Esho around 2018, who observed that patients had shifted from bringing photos of celebrities to bringing edited images of themselves.[1][3] A 2026 article in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology addresses the role of dermatologists in responding to social media dysmorphia.[2]

chain: Filters and edits create an idealised version of a face
Gap between filtered and real face shapes what people request
Clearer expectations lead to more realistic treatment and grooming goals
angle.text: Understanding the filter gap helps people judge how they look in unedited mirror and camera conditions, so that skincare, grooming and procedure goals are set against realistic reference images.

infobox: Informal term, not a formal diagnosis[1]

paras: Filters on apps such as Snapchat and Instagram can smooth skin, narrow noses and enlarge eyes in real time, producing an idealised version of the user's face.[1] Commentators say this can set unrealistic standards and widen the perceived gap between a person's actual and filtered appearance.[1] A related aesthetic, sometimes called "Instagram Face", is described as combining features such as high cheekbones, poreless skin and a small nose.[1]

Esho has said that patients previously presented photos of celebrities or models as reference images, but by the late 2010s many brought heavily edited selfies.[1] Researchers at Boston Medical Center also linked the rise of Snapchat, launched in 2011, to patients requesting surgery to look like filtered images.[1] Wikipedia's BDD article dates the coining of the term to 2018.[3]

BDD is described as an overwhelming preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance and sits in the obsessive-compulsive spectrum. It usually begins in adolescence. Wikipedia lists cognitive behavioural therapy and SSRI antidepressants as effective treatments, and notes that cosmetic surgery often fails to relieve BDD symptoms, so it recommends that surgeons and psychiatrists screen patients together.[3]

A 2019 study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery (Chen and colleagues) reported that people who used image-focused platforms and photo-editing apps were more likely to consider cosmetic surgery.[1] A 2015 study by McLean and colleagues found adolescent girls who edited photos of themselves and invested heavily in their images reported more body preoccupation and eating concerns.[1] A systematic review by Ryding and Kuss (2019) examined links between social networking use, body dissatisfaction and BDD.[1] Most of these studies are observational, so they do not establish causation. A 2022 survey by the American Academy of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery reported that most surveyed surgeons had patients seeking improvement for selfie appearance.[1]

Body image researcher Jasmine Fardouly has argued that negative body image is strongly tied to photo editing.[1] The authors of the JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery paper urged surgeons to screen patients for BDD before operating, and clinical commentary cited on Wikipedia states that cosmetic surgery is not a treatment for BDD.[1] Some of the statistics widely quoted in coverage originate from advocacy campaigns rather than peer-reviewed studies.[1]

In August 2020 Instagram banned filters that directly promote cosmetic surgery, after criticism of a filter that let users mark up their faces as a surgeon would.[1] Dove's #NoDigitalDistortion campaign aims to build self-esteem among young people.[1] Critics have said platform owners have done little more to limit distortion filters.[1]

Filtered and edited faces are part of the background against which online appearance communities discuss looks, ratings and procedures. On T Nation, a coach in a 2021 Q&A said social media "definitely contributes to body dysmorphia" and that easy manipulation of images does not help.[4]

timeline.event: McLean et al. study on photo editing and body concerns in adolescent girls.[1]
Tijion Esho coins the term "Snapchat dysmorphia".[3]
Chen et al. report in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery on social media use and consideration of cosmetic surgery.[1]
Instagram bans filters that directly promote cosmetic surgery.[1]

card.summary: Informal name for wanting to look like your filtered selfie; linked in studies to body dissatisfaction and surgery interest, but not a formal diagnosis.
card.aka: Snapchat dysmorphia, filter dysmorphia, selfie dysmorphia
card.note: Evidence is mostly correlational; not a formal diagnosis.

quick.overview:
Social media dysmorphia describes people feeling distress about, or seeking cosmetic procedures to match, their filtered selfies. The term was coined by surgeon Tijion Esho.

It is an informal label, not a diagnosis, and is discussed alongside body dysmorphic disorder.
quick.mechanism: Filters smooth skin and reshape features in real time, which commentators say creates an idealised self-image that real appearance cannot match. Observational studies link photo editing and image-focused platform use to body dissatisfaction.
quick.risks: Researchers link heavy editing and platform use to body preoccupation and surgery consideration, though causation is unproven. Surgeons are urged to screen for BDD, and cosmetic surgery is not considered a treatment for it.
